162.title: The self that is not slain (2.11–2.25)
162.hook: Krishna's first real teaching is about who is actually standing on the field, and it starts with clothes
162.howItsDone: Gita 2.20 and 2.22–2.23, on the self that is never born and never dies, are often recited at Hindu funerals and in times of grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday, uttishtha: cast it off, and stand up. And Arjuna said, teach me. Today, the teaching starts.

Find a photo of yourself at five. Much of that little body has been rebuilt since. The face, the voice, the height, what you're afraid of, what you love. And yet you point at it and say: that's me. Something was there at five, and at fifteen, and is here right now, listening. What is it? Arjuna is grieving for the people on the field. Krishna's first move is to ask who, exactly, is on the field.
screen: `A PHOTO OF YOU AT FIVE.` → `EVERYTHING CHANGED. THAT'S ME.` → `WHAT CARRIED OVER?`

segments.voice: You grieve for those who shouldn't be grieved for, Krishna says, and yet you speak like someone wise. The wise don't grieve for the living or the dead. There was never a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these kings, and there will never be a time when we cease to be. Then the picture from your photo. Just as the one who lives in this body passes through childhood, youth and old age, it passes on to another body. The wise aren't confused by it. Cold and heat, pleasure and pain, come and go. Bear them. What lasts, Krishna says, is the self, the atman, the one who lives in the body. In Sanskrit: na jayate mriyate va kadachin. It is not born, it does not die, at any time. Edwin Arnold, in 1885, turned it into verse: "Never the spirit was born; the spirit shall cease to be never; Never was time it was not; End and Beginning are dreams!" Then the everyday picture. As a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the self throws off worn-out bodies and takes on new ones. Nainam chhindanti shastrani, nainam dahati pavakah. Weapons don't cut it. Fire doesn't burn it. Water doesn't wet it. Wind doesn't dry it. Hindu schools read this differently. Some hear one Self in everyone. Others hear many eternal selves, pointing to that line: nor you, nor these kings. Readers have also long wrestled with the fact that it's said on a battlefield. But its first job is plain: to tell a grieving man that what he loves in them is not what arrows reach.
screen: `THE WISE DON'T GRIEVE THE LIVING OR DEAD.` · `CHILDHOOD, YOUTH, AGE, ANOTHER BODY.` · `NEVER BORN, NEVER DIES.` · `WORN-OUT CLOTHES, THROWN OFF.` · then, large: `WEAPONS DON'T CUT IT. FIRE DOESN'T BURN IT.`

segments.voice: Notice a sensation, the chair under you, then a thought, then a feeling, and watch each one come and go. Then, gently, notice what's noticing, the thing that was there at five and is here now, and rest as it for a few breaths without grabbing or naming it. In the Gita's picture, heat and cold, pleasure and pain keep passing through, and the one watching them doesn't come and go.
Atman. The self, the one who lives in the body: never born, never dies, and no weapon reaches it.
Your line: never born, never dies. Old clothes, same wearer. That's day one hundred sixty-two.

163.title: Duty and the coward (2.26–2.38)
163.hook: Krishna comes down from eternity to earth: death is certain, this is your work, and people will talk
163.tomorrow: "You have the right to act, never to the fruit" (2.39–2.53)
163.howItsDone: Hindus often draw on Gita 2.31–2.38 when speaking of svadharma, the duty that belongs to one's own role and stage of life, and 2.38's call to treat gain and loss, victory and defeat alike is widely quoted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, atman: the self that's never born and never dies, and bodies like worn-out clothes. Today, Krishna comes down to earth.

Good teachers do something you'll recognize. They give you the big, beautiful idea, see on your face that it hasn't landed, and try again from a plainer angle, closer to the ground. Krishna has just told Arjuna about the eternal self, weapons that can't cut it, fire that can't burn it. Arjuna is still sitting there. So Krishna changes gear. Suppose, he says in effect, you don't believe any of that. Here's why you still shouldn't grieve, and why you still have to stand up.
screen: `THE BIG IDEA DIDN'T LAND.` → `KRISHNA CHANGES GEAR.` → `SUPPOSE YOU DON'T BELIEVE IT.`

segments.voice: Argument one: even if you think the self is born and dies all the time, still don't grieve. In Sanskrit: jatasya hi dhruvo mrityur, dhruvam janma mritasya cha. For the one who is born, death is certain; for the one who dies, birth is certain. You can't change what's inevitable. Beings are unseen before they're born, seen in the middle, and unseen again at the end. What is there to lament? Argument two: dharma. Look at your svadharma, Krishna says, the duty that's yours. Arjuna is a kshatriya, a warrior whose role is to protect, and this, Krishna says, is a righteous fight. Refuse it, and you abandon what's yours. Argument three stings: people will talk. The great warriors will think you ran from fear. Your enemies will say things that shouldn't be said. For someone honored, dishonor is worse than death. These three get more and more down to earth. Commentators notice it too; some say Krishna is meeting Arjuna where he is, before the deeper teaching. Then the verse that turns toward it: sukha dukhe same kritva, labhalabhau jayajayau. Treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as the same, and then act. Readers take this battlefield in different ways. Some read it as a real war and a real duty. Gandhi read the whole Gita as a teaching about an inner fight, and drew nonviolence from it. Either way, the core holds: there's work that's yours, and running from it doesn't make you free.

segments.voice: Think of one role you actually hold, parent, friend, nurse, student, the one who keeps the family talking, and ask what piece of work in it only you can do, and you've been avoiding; don't judge it, just see it clearly. Then try on Krishna's line, win or lose, the same, and picture doing that work without needing it to go well, just because it's yours.
Svadharma. One's own duty, the work that's yours. Death is certain for the born, there's work that's yours, and win or lose, you do it anyway.
Your line: do what's yours. Win or lose, it's still yours. Day one hundred sixty-three, done.

screen: `DAY 163 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE RIGHT TO ACT, NOT THE FRUIT.`

164.title: "You have the right to act, never to the fruit" (2.39–2.53)
164.hook: the most quoted line in the Gita, the one on posters and in commencement speeches, and what it actually says
164.howItsDone: Gita 2.47, karmany evadhikaras te, is one of the most memorized verses in Hindu life; many Hindus recite it before work or exams, and 2.48 and 2.50 are often quoted as the Gita's definitions of yoga.

segments.voice: Yesterday, svadharma: death is certain for the born, and there's work that's yours. Today, the line.

You've probably met this verse without knowing it. On a poster in a yoga studio, in a graduation speech, on a mug: do your work, and don't worry about the results. It sounds like a nice bit of stress advice. It's stranger, and more demanding. It comes in the middle of Krishna's second chapter, just after he tells Arjuna, now I'll teach you a different way of seeing. And a man on a battlefield needed it more than anyone with a mug.
screen: `ON A POSTER, A MUG, A SPEECH.` → `STRESS ADVICE?` → `STRANGER, AND HARDER.`

segments.voice: Krishna starts with a promise. In this path, he says, no effort is ever lost, and even a little of it protects you from great fear. Then he warns about a certain kind of religion, full of flowery words and rituals performed to get rewards. Then the line itself, chapter two, verse forty-seven. In Sanskrit: karmany evadhikaras te, ma phaleshu kadachana. Your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits. And he keeps going, which the posters usually don't. Ma karma phala hetur bhur: don't let the fruit be your motive. Ma te sango 'stv akarmani: and don't be attached to not acting, either. Krishna isn't saying care less. You get the doing; the results were never yours to own. Plant the tree, water the tree, protect the tree. Whether it fruits, and who eats the fruit, belongs to something larger. And Arjuna can't use that as a reason to sit down, because not acting is just another attachment. Then Krishna gives it a name. Samatvam yoga uchyate. Evenness is called yoga: steady in success, steady in failure. Two verses later, a second famous definition: yogah karmasu kaushalam. Yoga is skill in action. So yoga, in the Gita, isn't first a posture. It's a way of working: fully, well, and without clutching. For Arjuna, frozen because of what the fight will cost, this is the first way out. He doesn't have to control how it ends. He has to do what's his, well, with his hands open.
screen: `NO EFFORT IS EVER LOST.` · `YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE ACTION ALONE.` · `NOT ATTACHED TO NOT ACTING EITHER.` · `EVENNESS IS YOGA. SKILL IN ACTION.` · then, large: `THE DOING IS YOURS. THE FRUIT ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and think of something you're working hard on, and how badly you want it to turn out a certain way. Keep the work, the next email, the next rehearsal, the next honest conversation, and let go of the outcome. Each time you breathe out, let your palms soften a little more.
Adhikara. Your right. Karmany evadhikaras te: your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits.
Your line: the line. Karmany evadhikaras te: the doing is yours, the fruit isn't. Until tomorrow.

165.title: The steady one (2.54–2.61)
165.hook: Arjuna asks the most practical question in the book: what does a person like that actually look like?
165.tomorrow: Desire → anger → ruin; the peace at the end (2.62–2.72)
165.howItsDone: The verses on the sthitaprajna, the one of steady wisdom (Gita 2.54–2.72), are recited daily in some Hindu homes, and were recited at the prayer meetings in Gandhi's ashram.

segments.voice: Yesterday, adhikara: your right is to the action alone, never to the fruit. Today, Arjuna asks what a steady person looks like.

Some people are like this. A grandmother, a nurse on the night shift, a coach, a friend. When the room goes crazy, they don't. Bad news comes, and they take it in, and they're still themselves. Good news comes, and they're glad, and still themselves. Arjuna has just heard Krishna talk about evenness, about acting with open hands. So he asks the obvious question. What does such a person look like? How do they talk? How do they sit? How do they walk?
screen: `THE ONE WHO DOESN'T GO CRAZY.` → `STILL THEMSELVES.` → `HOW DO THEY TALK, SIT, WALK?`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit, Arjuna's question begins: sthitaprajnasya ka bhasha. What is the description of the one whose wisdom is steady? Sthita, standing firm. Prajna, wisdom. Krishna's answer isn't a list of rules. It's a portrait. When someone lets go of all the cravings that swirl in the mind, and is content in the self, by the self, that one is steady. Then the heart of it: duhkheshv anudvigna manah, sukheshu vigata sprihah. The one whose mind isn't shaken in sorrow, who doesn't crave in pleasure, free from clinging, fear and anger: that's a sage of steady mind. Not someone who feels nothing. Someone who isn't knocked over. Then a picture from nature. Like a tortoise drawing in its limbs from every side, the steady one can draw the senses back from the things that pull at them. The tortoise still has legs, and uses them. It just isn't dragged around by them. Then Krishna says something honest. If you just stop eating, the objects of the senses fall away, but the taste for them stays. Only when a person sees something higher does even the taste go. And the senses are strong: they can carry off the mind of even a wise person who's trying. So sit, he says, with your mind on me. This isn't willpower alone. These verses meant a great deal to Gandhi, who had them recited at the prayer meetings in his ashram: a portrait to measure yourself by, gently, every evening.
screen: `STHITAPRAJNA: STEADY WISDOM.` · `UNSHAKEN IN SORROW, UNCRAVING IN JOY.` · `LIKE A TORTOISE DRAWING IN.` · `THE TASTE STAYS. SEE SOMETHING HIGHER.` · then, large: `NOT KNOCKED OVER.`

segments.voice: Notice everything pulling at your senses: sounds, the phone nearby, an itch, a smell from the kitchen. Then, like a tortoise drawing in its legs, gently draw your attention back to the breath, hearing but not reaching toward sounds, feeling but not chasing sensations, and rest there, shell and all. When something pulls you out, and it will, don't be annoyed; just draw in again.
Sthitaprajna. The one whose wisdom is steady: unshaken in sorrow, uncraving in joy, drawing in the senses like a tortoise.
Your line: unmoved. Still feeling everything, just not knocked over by it. One hundred sixty-five days now.

166.title: Desire → anger → ruin; the peace at the end (2.62–2.72)
166.hook: eight links from a passing thought to losing yourself, and then an ocean that rivers pour into without changing
166.howItsDone: Gita 2.62–2.63, the chain from dwelling on objects to ruin, is often taught in Hindu moral teaching, and the closing verses of chapter two, on the ocean and on peace, are recited in some homes as part of the sthitaprajna verses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sthitaprajna: unshaken in sorrow, uncraving in joy, drawing in like a tortoise. Today, how steadiness gets lost, and where it ends.

Someone is scrolling, and there it is. A jacket, a car, somebody's vacation, somebody's job. A second's thought. Then another, later. By evening, wanting. By the weekend, not having it is quietly annoying. Then someone at dinner says the wrong thing, and the snap comes out of nowhere, and nobody's sure why. Long before phones, the Gita laid out that exact slide, link by link, in two verses. Then it shows the way out.
screen: `SCROLLING, AND THERE IT IS.` → `BY EVENING, WANTING IT.` → `A SNAP AT DINNER. WHY?`

segments.voice: Verses sixty-two and sixty-three. In Sanskrit the chain begins: dhyayato vishayan pumsah, sangas teshupajayate. When a person dwells on the objects of the senses, attachment to them is born. From attachment, desire, kama. From desire, anger, krodha, because desire that's blocked turns into anger. From anger, delusion. From delusion, memory wanders: you forget what you know, who you are. From the loss of memory, the power of discernment is destroyed. And when discernment is destroyed, the person is lost. Eight links, from dwelling on a thing to ruin. Notice where it starts: not with doing anything wrong, but with dwelling. The chain begins in attention, which means it can be broken at the very first link. Then Krishna turns to the end of the chain, the peace. The one who moves among the things of the world with the senses under control, free of grasping and aversion, finds clarity, prasada, and in that clarity all sorrows end. For the unsteady there's no peace, and without peace, how can there be happiness? Then an image from the coast. The ocean is filled by rivers from every side, and yet it stays within its shores, unmoved. So the one into whom desires flow like rivers, and who stays unmoved, finds peace; not the one who chases desires. And the final verse: the one who lets go of desires, free of I and mine, attains peace. This is the Brahman state, Krishna says. Whoever reaches it, even at the very end, finds the stillness of Brahman. And that's chapter two, the chapter that holds everything.

167.title: Why not just renounce? (3.1–3.9)
167.hook: Arjuna spots what looks like a loophole: if understanding is better than action, why not skip the action?
167.howItsDone: Chapter three of the Gita, Karma Yoga, is often taught as the foundation of the householder's spiritual life in Hinduism: work, family and duty done without attachment, as an offering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, krodha: the chain that starts with dwelling, and the ocean that stays in its shores. Today, chapter three, and a sharp question.

Arjuna has been listening carefully, and like any sharp student, he's found what looks like a contradiction. Krishna, you keep praising understanding, steady wisdom, a mind free of desire. You say that's higher than action. So why push me into this terrible action? Your words are mixed. You're confusing me. Just tell me the one thing that's best. It's a modern question, too. If peace is the goal, why not quit? Leave the job, the city, the argument, and go sit on a mountain.
screen: `IF WISDOM IS HIGHER, WHY ACT?` → `YOUR WORDS ARE MIXED.` → `WHY NOT QUIT, AND SIT ON A MOUNTAIN?`

segments.voice: Krishna says there are two paths in this world, both taught long ago: the path of knowledge, for those given to contemplation, and the path of action, for those given to work. Then he closes the loophole. Not by avoiding action does anyone get free of action, and not by renouncing alone does anyone reach perfection. In Sanskrit: na hi kashchit kshanam api jatu tishthaty akarmakrit. No one, not even for a moment, can remain without acting. You breathe. You blink. Your heart beats. Your nature keeps moving you whether you like it or not. So the choice was never action or no action. It's what kind. Someone who holds the body still but keeps dwelling in the mind on the things they gave up, the text calls a mithyachara, a pretender, someone whose outward conduct is a lie. Better, he says, the one who controls the senses with the mind and gets to work, unattached. Then: niyatam kuru karma tvam, karma jyayo hy akarmanah. Do the work that's yours; action is better than inaction. You couldn't even keep your body alive without acting. And the verse that opens tomorrow: the world is bound by action, except action done as yajna, as an offering. So act, Krishna says, for that, free from attachment. The Gita honors renunciation; Hindu tradition has great renouncers. But it won't let running away pass for freedom. In Krishna's answer, the mountain doesn't save anyone from their own mind. What frees is how one acts.

Karma. Action, work, deed: chapter three is Karma Yoga, the yoga of action. No one can stop acting, even for a moment; freedom isn't escaping action, it's how you act.
Your line: act anyway. The question was never whether to act, but how. See you tomorrow.

168.title: The wheel of sacrifice (3.10–3.16)
168.hook: food, rain, offering, action, and back again: a wheel the world turns on, and a hard word for anyone who only takes
168.howItsDone: Many Hindus offer food to God before eating and set a portion aside for guests, animals or those in need; Gita 3.13, on eating what remains after the offering, and 3.14's wheel of food, rain and sacrifice are often cited to explain these customs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma: no one can stop acting, even for a moment, so the question is how. Today, what the acting is for.

Breakfast this morning, whatever it was: toast, rice, coffee. Follow it backward. Somebody sold it to you, somebody drove it there, somebody harvested it. It grew because rain fell and sun shone and someone planted and weeded. And that farmer ate food someone else grew. Keep going and there's no beginning, just a circle of people and weather and earth, each handing something on. The Gita gave that circle a name. And it has a very blunt word for anyone who eats from it without handing anything back.
screen: `FOLLOW YOUR BREAKFAST BACKWARD.` → `A CIRCLE WITH NO BEGINNING.` → `A BLUNT WORD FOR TAKERS.`

segments.voice: Krishna tells a story of the beginning. The creator, Prajapati, brought forth beings together with yajna, sacrifice, offering, and said: by this you'll flourish; let this be your wish-fulfilling cow. Nourish the gods with it, and the gods will nourish you. Nourishing one another, you'll reach the highest good. Then the blunt word. Whoever enjoys the gifts given, without offering anything back, is a stena. A thief. The good who eat what's left after the offering are freed from wrong. But those who cook only for themselves, bhunjate te tv agham papa, eat wrong itself. Now the wheel. In Sanskrit: annad bhavanti bhutani, parjanyad anna sambhavah, yajnad bhavati parjanyo, yajnah karma samudbhavah. From food, beings come to be. From rain, food. From sacrifice, rain. And sacrifice is born of action. Whoever doesn't help turn the wheel set turning like this, Krishna says, lives in vain. In the Vedic world yajna meant fire rituals, offerings poured into the flame; Hindus still perform them, as homa or havan. But the Gita widens the word as it goes; by chapter four it counts many kinds of work as yajna. So it's the family cooking and first setting some aside for God, or for a guest, or for the cow outside. It's the practice from camp three, food offered, then shared. And that's this week: the self never slain, the duty that's yours, the line about the fruit, sthitaprajna, the chain and its end, act anyway, and now yajna, the wheel. In the Gita's picture, every act is either a turn of the wheel or a theft from it.
screen: `CREATED TOGETHER WITH OFFERING.` · `WHO ONLY TAKES IS A THIEF.` · `FOOD, RAIN, OFFERING, ACTION.` · `YAJNA WIDENS: WORK AS OFFERING.` · then, large: `TURN THE WHEEL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you received today, food, a kindness, a paycheck, warm water, and follow it backward, hand to hand: the driver, the farmer, the rain. Then look forward and ask who's downstream of you, and what you'll hand on. If you pray, you can offer the day's first bite before you eat it.
Yajna. Sacrifice, offering: first the Vedic fire rite, then in the Gita any action given, not grabbed. Food from rain, rain from offering, offering from action.
Your line: give back. Food, rain, offering, action: the wheel keeps turning. A full week, done.
